title: GLP-1 Drugs Like Ozempic Are Now Linked to Smell and Taste Disturbances — and the Implications Go Beyond Food
excerpt: A study of nearly 900,000 diabetes patients found that GLP-1 users had an 81% higher risk of smell dysfunction and a 52% higher risk of taste changes — subtle shifts that doctors say are early markers of neurological health.
body:
The list of known GLP-1 side effects — nausea, diarrhoea, the so-called "Ozempic face" — has grown familiar to the millions of people now taking drugs like semaglutide and tirzepatide. But a large new study published in *JAMA Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery* has surfaced a less discussed risk: the drugs may quietly alter how users smell and taste the world around them.

Researchers at Hebrew University in Jerusalem analysed electronic health records from nearly 900,000 patients with type 2 diabetes, collected between 2017 and 2026. Half were on GLP-1 receptor agonists; the other half used other diabetes medications. None had pre-existing smell or taste impairments.

Over two years of follow-up, GLP-1 users were **81 per cent more likely** to develop smell disturbances and **52 per cent more likely** to report taste disturbances compared to the control group. The conditions ranged from anosmia (complete loss of smell) to parosmia (where pleasant scents suddenly smell chemical or rotten) to parageusia (phantom or distorted tastes).

## The Numbers Are Small — but the Signal Matters

The absolute rates were low: 0.37 per cent of GLP-1 users developed sensory disturbances, versus 0.22 per cent in the control group. In a clinical trial, that gap might seem negligible. But with over 30 million Americans now estimated to be on GLP-1 drugs — and that number rising sharply — even a fraction of a per cent translates to tens of thousands of people experiencing changes to two of their most intimate senses.

"Smell and taste are subtle but critical markers of systemic well-being," noted an editorial published alongside the study. The editorial was particularly pointed about smell dysfunction being "one of the most reliable warning signs of neurodegenerative conditions" — raising the question of whether GLP-1-related sensory changes could mask or mimic early signs of conditions like Parkinson's or Alzheimer's.

## Why This Matters Beyond the Dinner Table

The editorial made a broader observation that will resonate with anyone who has built a life around food, family, and cultural ritual. GLP-1 drugs that alter "the sensory world that surrounds eating" don't just change what a meal tastes like — they may change "the way in which we experience travel, family gatherings, milestones, and the family dinner."

For patients with uncontrolled diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or severe obesity, the trade-off may be worth it, the editorial acknowledged. But for those using the drugs for "marginal weight loss or cosmetic purposes," the risk calculus shifts.

A separate study from the University of Pennsylvania, published earlier in 2026, offered corroborating evidence using direct sensory testing. In a controlled comparison of 46 GLP-1 users and 46 matched controls, 85 per cent of GLP-1 users scored worse on standardised taste tests — across all five basic taste qualities: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. Smell function was also slightly reduced, though not to statistically significant levels.

## The South Asian Angle

The findings carry particular weight for the Indian diaspora. South Asians have among the highest rates of type 2 diabetes globally — an estimated 11 per cent prevalence among Indian Americans, roughly double the rate for white Americans — meaning GLP-1 prescriptions are disproportionately common in this community.

The cultural stakes are also higher. In South Asian households, food is the connective tissue of daily life: the smell of tadka hitting hot oil, the layered aromatics of a biryani, the specific sweetness of a mithai made for Diwali. Losing the ability to fully experience these sensory textures isn't a medical footnote — it's a quality-of-life issue that touches identity.

The study's authors called for "closer monitoring and greater public health awareness," along with research into the biological mechanisms at play. GLP-1 receptors are widely distributed throughout the nervous system, including in brainstem areas that process taste and in the vagus nerve — suggesting the sensory effects may be a direct pharmacological consequence, not an incidental one.

## What to Do If You're on a GLP-1 Drug

Doctors aren't suggesting patients stop their medication based on this data alone. But the findings do argue for a conversation — particularly if you've noticed food tasting different, scents seeming muted, or flavours that once brought pleasure now landing flat. These changes can be gradual enough to dismiss as ageing or stress, but they deserve clinical attention.

If smell or taste changes emerge, a referral to an otolaryngologist for formal sensory testing can help distinguish GLP-1-related effects from other causes. And for anyone considering starting a GLP-1 drug purely for modest weight loss rather than metabolic necessity, the study adds one more factor to weigh.
